an4.171:1.3: The tag _avijjāpaccayāva_ (variant _-ca_) is odd here and appears outside the normal syntax. It is also found in the parallel at [sn12.25:10.3](). Perhaps the purpose is to clarify that the mere presence of body, speech, and mind is not sufficient for kammic intentions, as arahants have body, speech, and mind but do not make kamma. See on this topic also the closing section.
an4.171:2.2: This anticipates the Abhidhamma term _sasaṅkhārika_, intentions that are prompted or instigated by another. For example, one might feel hungry and say, “Let’s eat”. Or someone else might say to you, “Let’s eat”. In both cases there is still moral responsibility for choices, but in the latter it is to some degree mitigated.
an4.171:2.3: “Deliberate” (_sampajāna_) means one is aware before, during, and after ([mn61:12.1](), [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc1:2.2.2]()). Compare the legal concept “pre-meditated”.
an4.171:5.2: The sentence has a conditional structure which limits and specifies its application. The body has not disappeared. Rather, it is *that* body, namely the one dependent on ignorance, which no longer exists to create kamma. Further, the sentence is an exemplification of the concept of specific conditionality: *this* body ceases, and *that* pleasure and pain no longer arise. An arahant experiences pleasure and pain as a result of past life choices, but does not actively create new kammic feelings.
an4.171:5.3: Up to here, this discourse is identical with [sn12.25](), which ends at this point. The identity even extends to the ending, which in both cases has a close _-ti_ indicating end of quote. The following portion then begins exactly like a normal Aṅguttara sutta. It seems as if the first portion has been rather clumsily edited in. I retain the quote marks to indicate this.
